claim: Rapidly growing budding yeast contain about 190,000 ribosomes.
source: Rapidly growing budding yeast, for example, contain about 190,000 ribosomes (von der Haar, 2008), each of which requires the production of over a hundred different proteins.
evidence: Supported by citation to von der Haar, 2008

claim: Approximately 30% of the proteome of rapidly growing cells encodes for ribosomal proteins.
source: Overall, ≈30% of the proteome of rapidly growing cells encodes for ribosomal proteins and ≈80% of all cellular RNA encodes for the rRNA components of the ribosomes (Warner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner, 1999

claim: Approximately 80% of all cellular RNA encodes for the rRNA components of the ribosomes.
source: Overall, ≈30% of the proteome of rapidly growing cells encodes for ribosomal proteins and ≈80% of all cellular RNA encodes for the rRNA components of the ribosomes (Warner, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Warner, 1999

claim: Resource allocation models predict that growth rate is maximized when all expressed ribosomal proteins are fully employed in protein translation.
source: These models predict that growth rate is maximized when all expressed ribosomal proteins are fully employed in protein translation (Bosdriesz et al., 2015; Dekel and Alon, 2005; Kafri et al., 2016a; Keren et al., 2013; Klumpp et al., 2013; Koch, 1988; Maaløe, 1979; Scott and Hwa, 2011; Scott et al., 2010; 2014; Vind et al., 1993).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to theoretical models

claim: Slow-growing bacteria contain excess ribosomes that are not actively translating.
source: However, recent studies suggest that while this model may hold in rapidly growing bacteria, slow-growing bacteria do contain excess ribosomes that are not actively translating (Dai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dai et al., 2016

claim: In rapidly growing budding yeast, protein translation is not universally limiting for protein production and growth rate.
source: Further, we recently reported that in rapidly growing budding yeast, protein translation is not universally limiting for protein production and growth rate (Kafri et al., 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kafri et al., 2016b

claim: The ribosome content of bacteria growing in different environments increases linearly with growth rate, independently of the specifics of each nutrient.
source: Consistent with its major role in driving cell growth, the ribosome content of bacteria growing in different environments increases linearly with growth rate, independently of the specifics of each nutrient (Brauer et al., 2008; Bremer and Ehrenberg, 1995; Nomura et al., 1984; Schaechter et al., 1958; Scott et al., 2010; Waldron and Lacroute, 1975; Warner, 1999; Zaslaver et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to bacterial studies

claim: Cells produce excess ribosomal proteins, amounting to a constant ≈8% of the proteome.
source: We find that cells produce excess ribosomal proteins, amounting to a constant ≈8% of the proteome.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data presented in the study

claim: Approximately 25% of ribosomal proteins expressed in rapidly growing cells does not contribute to translation.
source: Accordingly, ≈25% of ribosomal proteins expressed in rapidly growing cells does not contribute to translation.
evidence: Inferred from the measured ribosomal fraction and polysome profiling data

claim: The fraction of inactive ribosomal proteins increases as growth rate decreases.
source: Further, this fraction increases as growth rate decreases and these excess ribosomal proteins are employed when translation demands unexpectedly increase.
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data across different growth conditions

claim: Excess ribosomal proteins are employed when translation demands unexpectedly increase.
source: Further, this fraction increases as growth rate decreases and these excess ribosomal proteins are employed when translation demands unexpectedly increase.
evidence: Supported by nutrient upshift experiments and exit from stationary phase data

claim: Proteome profiles cluster into two dominating groups depending on whether cells grew in a fermentative or respiratory mode.
source: Examining the Pearson correlation between the different profiles (Figure 1A), we observed that profiles were classified into two dominating clusters, depending on whether cells grew in a fermentative or respiratory mode.
evidence: Supported by Pearson correlation analysis shown in Figure 1A

claim: Correlations between profiles within the same cluster were ≈0.7–0.9.
source: Correlations between profiles within the same cluster were ≈0.7–0.9, while correlations between profiles assigned to different clusters were lower but still substantial (0.3–0.6).
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix data in Figure 1A

claim: Correlations between profiles assigned to different clusters were 0.3–0.6.
source: Correlations between profiles within the same cluster were ≈0.7–0.9, while correlations between profiles assigned to different clusters were lower but still substantial (0.3–0.6).
evidence: Supported by correlation matrix data in Figure 1A

claim: Division times of cells in the 15 conditions examined varied between 1.5 to 6.5 hr.
source: Division times of cells in the 15 conditions we examined varied between 1.5 to 6.5 hr.
evidence: Supported by growth rate measurements across different conditions

claim: In standard media, the proteome was dominated by translation-related factors (≈40%) and glycolytic proteins (≈15%).
source: In standard media, the proteome was dominated by translation-related factors (≈40%) and glycolytic proteins (≈15%) (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The fraction of glycolytic proteins remained largely invariant between conditions.
source: The fraction of glycolytic proteins remained largely invariant between conditions, while the translation-related fraction decreased with growth rate, reaching ≈15% in slow-growing cells.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data across conditions

claim: The translation-related fraction decreased with growth rate, reaching ≈15% in slow-growing cells.
source: The fraction of glycolytic proteins remained largely invariant between conditions, while the translation-related fraction decreased with growth rate, reaching ≈15% in slow-growing cells.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data across conditions

claim: Mitochondrial proteins double in quantity to ≈20% of the proteome in slow growing cells.
source: Mitochondrial proteins, for example, double in quantity to ≈20% of the proteome in the slow growing cells, in accordance with the increased reliance of these cells on respiration (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data shown in Figure 1C

claim: The proteome fraction coding for ribosomal proteins increased linearly with growth rate, from ≈8% in the slowest growing cells to ≈30% in rapidly growing cells.
source: The proteome fraction coding for this group increased linearly with growth rate, irrespective of the specific media, from ≈8% in the slowest growing cells to ≈30% in rapidly growing cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data shown in Figure 2A

claim: Budding yeast show a similar growth law to that previously described in bacteria.
source: Therefore, budding yeast show a similar growth law to that previously described in bacteria.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of the linear scaling relationship with bacterial literature

claim: The fraction of mRNA transcripts that code for ribosomal proteins as a function of cell growth rate showed the same quantitative scaling as observed at the level of the proteome.
source: Notably, plotting the fraction of mRNA transcripts that code for ribosomal proteins as a function of cell growth rate showed the same quantitative scaling as observed at the level of the proteome (Figure 2B top).
evidence: Supported by transcriptome profiling data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Regulation of the ribosomal protein fraction with growth rate depends almost exclusively on mRNA transcription.
source: Thus, regulation of the ribosomal protein fraction with growth rate depends almost exclusively on mRNA transcription.
evidence: Inferred from the quantitative agreement between transcriptome and proteome scaling

claim: The ribosomal fraction follows growth rate with the same qualitative scaling when comparing different strains growing in the same condition.
source: Examining the transcription profiles of these strains, we find that the ribosomal fraction follows growth rate with the same qualitative scaling as observed when comparing growth rates in different conditions (Figure 2B, top).
evidence: Supported by transcription profiling data of different yeast strains

claim: The general scaling relationship between ribosome content and growth rate is conserved when comparing the same strain across conditions and when comparing different strains growing in the same condition.
source: The general scaling relationship between ribosome content and growth rate is therefore conserved not only when comparing the same strain across conditions, but also when comparing different strains growing in the same condition.
evidence: Supported by transcription profiling data across strains and conditions

claim: The scaling of ribosome content and growth rate is largely lost following genetic perturbations that affect cell growth.
source: Notably, in this case, the scaling between ribosome content and growth rate was largely lost (Figure 2B, bottom); in fact, most mutants that reduced growth rate had a minor effect on the expression of genes coding for ribosomal proteins.
evidence: Supported by analysis of deletion mutant data from Kemmeren et al., 2014 and O'Duibhir et al., 2014

claim: Most growth-affecting mutants express more ribosomal protein coding genes than expected given their growth rate.
source: As a result, growth-affecting mutations expressed more ribosomal protein coding genes than expected given their growth rate.
evidence: Inferred from the deviation from the scaling curve in deletion mutants

claim: The tight correlation between ribosome content and growth rate results from environmental signaling, rather than direct causal relationships.
source: This implies that the tight correlation between ribosome content and growth rate results from environmental signaling, rather than direct causal relationships (Levy et al., 2007).
evidence: Inferred from the loss of scaling in genetic mutants and supported by citation

claim: The translation elongation rate is 10.5 aa/sec.
source: We can estimate γ using measured parameters: the translation elongation rate (10.5 aa/sec) (Waldron et al., 1977) and the number of amino-acids composing the budding yeast ribosome (12,485 A.A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waldron et al., 1977

claim: The number of amino-acids composing the budding yeast ribosome is 12,485.
source: We can estimate γ using measured parameters: the translation elongation rate (10.5 aa/sec) (Waldron et al., 1977) and the number of amino-acids composing the budding yeast ribosome (12,485 A.A).
evidence: Based on known ribosome composition

claim: The estimated value of γ−1 is 20 min.
source: By this estimation, γ−1 = 20 min.
evidence: Calculated from translation elongation rate and ribosome size

claim: The predicted value of γ−1 is ≈30% smaller than the measured slope Δr/Δµ = 21/ln(2) min.
source: This predicted value is ≈30% smaller than our measured slope Δr/Δµ = 21/ln(2) min, (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: Comparison of calculated and measured values

claim: Arrested cells maintain a pool of inactive ribosomes.
source: Indeed, arrested cells were shown to maintain a pool of inactive ribosomes (Dai et al., 2016; van den Elzen et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dai et al., 2016 and van den Elzen et al., 2014

claim: The residual inactive ribosome fraction r0 can be estimated from the measured scaling curve, provided that the ribosome elongation rates γ are known.
source: Using the simplified model above, Equation (1), the fraction of this inactive pool r0 can be estimated from the measured scaling curve, provided that we know the ribosome elongation rates γ.
evidence: Based on theoretical model relating ribosome content to growth rate

claim: If elongation rate γ is constant and independent of growth rate, then the residual fraction remains a constant r0 = 8% at all growth rates.
source: If elongation rate γ is constant and γ is independent of growth rate, then the residual fraction also remains a constant r0 = 8% at all growth rate.
evidence: Derived from theoretical model assuming constant elongation rate

claim: Measured elongation rates in glucose and in media lacking nitrogen remain the same despite a two-fold reduction in growth rate.
source: In one report, measured elongation rates in glucose and in media lacking nitrogen remain the same despite a two-fold reduction in growth rate (Waldron et al., 1977).
evidence: Supported by citation to Waldron et al., 1977

claim: Elongation rates decrease by ≈40% in media lacking acetate compared to glucose.
source: By contrast, a second report suggested that elongation rates decrease by ≈40% in media lacking acetate (Bonven and Gulløv, 1979).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bonven and Gulløv, 1979

claim: A substantial inactive fraction (monosomes) was observed in fast growing cells (ρ = 0.18).
source: A substantial inactive fraction (monosomes) was observed in the fast growing cells (ρ = 0.18), which further increased in the slow-growing cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The inactive fraction of ribosomes further increased in slow-growing cells.
source: A substantial inactive fraction (monosomes) was observed in the fast growing cells (ρ = 0.18), which further increased in the slow-growing cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 3A

claim: The relative fraction of monosomes increased with decreasing growth rate.
source: Notably, the relative fraction of monosomes increased with decreasing growth rate.
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data across different growth conditions

claim: The fraction of monosomes was in quantitative agreement with the predicted fraction of inactive ribosomes assuming a constant residual r0 ≈8%.
source: Further, this fraction was in quantitative agreement with the predicted fraction of inactive ribosomes assuming a constant residual r0 ≈8% (Figure 3B).
evidence: Comparison of polysome profiling data with theoretical predictions

claim: During steady growth, cells devote a constant, ≈8% of their proteome to producing ribosomes that are not actively translating.
source: We conclude that during steady growth, cells devote a constant, ≈8% of their proteome to producing ribosomes that are not actively translating.
evidence: Supported by proteomic and polysome profiling data

claim: The fraction of ribosomes that are not actively translating ranges from ≈25% in rapidly growing cells and further increases with decreasing growth rate.
source: Therefore, the fraction of ribosomes that are not actively translating ranges from ≈25% in rapidly growing cells (r0≈8% relative to the total ribosomal fraction r≈30%) and further increases with decreasing growth rate (Figure 3B).
evidence: Calculated from proteomic and polysome profiling data

claim: Entering stationary phase requires an increased production of glycolytic enzymes.
source: Entering stationary phase represents such a scenario (Ju and Warner, 1994), as the reduced availability of nutrients requires an increased production of glycolytic enzymes (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, right column).
evidence: Supported by citation and proteomic data

claim: Ribosomal content decreased ≈2.5 generations (four hours) before growth rate dropped during entry into stationary phase.
source: Indeed, ribosomal content decreased ≈2.5 generations (four hours) before growth rate dropped (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data from Murphy et al., 2015

claim: Transcription profiling of cells shifted to low phosphate medium showed an early decrease in ribosomal protein transcripts, ~5 hr before growth rate was reduced.
source: Similarly, transcription profiling of cells shifted to low phosphate medium showed an early decrease in ribosomal protein transcripts, ~5 hr before growth rate was reduced (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: Supported by transcription profiling data

claim: Continuous cell cultures growing in a phosphate-limited chemostat responded to a spike of high phosphate within minutes.
source: First, we found that continuous cell cultures growing in a phosphate-limited chemostat responded to a spike of high phosphate within minutes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by chemostat experiment data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Cells transferred from galactose to glucose increase their growth rate from 0.36 gen/hr to 0.54 gen/hr within minutes of the transfer.
source: Second, using microfluidic-coupled microscopy, we followed individual cells transferred from galactose to glucose and observed that cells increase their growth rate from 0.36 gen/hr to 0.54 gen/hr within minutes of the transfer (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by microfluidic microscopy data shown in Figure 4C

claim: Cells increase their growth rate and protein production rates within a short time that appears insufficient for synthesizing new ribosomes.
source: Therefore, cells increase their growth rate and thus protein production rates within a short time that appears insufficient for synthesizing new ribosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the rapid response to nutrient upshift

claim: Cells resumed rapid growth of 0.55 gen/hr following a ≈40 min lag after transfer from early stationary phase to fresh media.
source: Cells resumed rapid growth of 0.55 gen/hr following a ≈40 min lag.
evidence: Supported by proteome profiling during exit from stationary phase

claim: Ribosome content did not change during the lag time after transfer to fresh media, but began to increase only after cells had attained fast growth.
source: Proteome profiling revealed that ribosome content did not change during the lag time, but began to increase only after cells had attained fast growth (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by proteome profiling data shown in Figure 4D

claim: Cells utilize the vast majority of expressed ribosomes to account for the observed growth rate during the initial growth phase after exiting stationary phase.
source: In fact, it appears that to account for the observed growth rate during this initial growth phase, cells need to utilize the vast majority of expressed ribosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the growth rate and ribosome content data during exit from stationary phase

claim: In all three conditions, growth rate and the ribosomal fraction r decreased with increasing mCherry levels.
source: As expected, in all three conditions, growth rate and the ribosomal fraction r decreased with increasing mCherry levels (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling of burden strains shown in Figure 5A

claim: Burden cells showed a scaling relation that was highly similar to that observed in wild-type cells when compared across conditions.
source: Burden cells showed a scaling relation that was highly similar to that observed in wild-type cells: when compared across conditions, ribosome content decreased linearly with growth rate.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling of burden strains across conditions

claim: The slope of the scaling curve was independent of the level of the burden.
source: Notably, the slope of this scaling curve was independent of the level of the burden, suggesting that ribosome translation rates γ remained invariant to the burden.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling of burden strains

claim: Ribosome translation rates γ remained invariant to the burden.
source: Notably, the slope of this scaling curve was independent of the level of the burden, suggesting that ribosome translation rates γ remained invariant to the burden.
evidence: Inferred from the constant slope of the scaling curve across burden levels

claim: The burden affected the residual r0, the predicted proteome fraction coding for non-translating ribosomes.
source: In contrast, the burden did affect the residual r0, the predicted proteome fraction coding for non-translating ribosomes.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling of burden strains

claim: In the zero-growth limit, ribosome content in high burden cells decreased from its wild-type value (r0 = 8.1%) to a lower value, r0 = 5.5%.
source: In this limit, ribosome content in high burden cells decreased from its wild-type value (r0 = 8.1%) to a lower value, r0 = 5.5% (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Burdened cells employ a higher fraction of their ribosomes, leaving a smaller pool of inactive ribosomes.
source: Therefore, the burdened cells employ a higher fraction of their ribosomes, leaving a smaller pool of inactive ribosomes.
evidence: Inferred from the reduced r0 in burden cells

claim: Burdened cells exit starvation with a delay.
source: Burdened cells exit starvation with a delay (Kafri et al., 2016b; Shachrai et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kafri et al., 2016b and Shachrai et al., 2010

claim: The delay in recovery from starvation increases linearly with the mCherry burden.
source: As expected, this delay increases linearly with the mCherry burden.
evidence: Supported by recovery time data from Kafri et al., 2016b

claim: The differences in recovery times were quantitatively explained by the difference in r0.
source: Notably, the differences in recovery times were quantitatively explained by the difference in r0; for example, the recovery time of eight-copy burden cells was prolonged by ≈15%, consistent with the corresponding ≈15% decrease in the measured r0.
evidence: Comparison of recovery time data with r0 measurements

claim: When comparing cells that grow in different conditions, the predicted ratio ra/r0 increases linearly with growth rate.
source: As a direct consequence of the scaling law, when comparing cells that grow in different conditions, the predicted ratio ra/r0 increases linearly with growth rate (Figure 6A).
evidence: Derived from the scaling law and shown in Figure 6A

claim: Comparing between wild-type and burden cells, the ratio ra/r0 is invariant to the burden and depends mainly on the growth condition.
source: However, comparing between wild-type and burden cells, we noted that this ratio is invariant to the burden and depends mainly on the growth condition (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data shown in Figure 6A

claim: The ratio of polysomes to monosome remains largely invariant between wild-type and burden cells growing in the same condition, despite their different growth rate.
source: As predicted, the ratio of polysomes to monosome remains largely invariant between wild-type and burden cells growing in the same condition, despite their different growth rate (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by polysome profiling data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The tuning of ribosome content and of the fraction of ribosomes that are actively translating depend primarily on signaling from the environment with little contribution of internal growth-rate dependent feedback.
source: Taken together, we propose that the tuning of ribosome content and of the fraction of ribosomes that are actively translating depend primarily on signaling from the environment with little contribution of internal growth-rate dependent feedback (Figure 7).
evidence: Inferred from the invariance of ra/r0 to burden and dependence on growth condition

claim: The correlation between ribosome parameters and growth rate is not direct, but rather results from evolutionarily tuned signaling.
source: Thus, although both parameters show a tight correlation with growth rate, this correlation is not direct, but rather results from evolutionarily tuned signaling.
evidence: Inferred from the dependence on environmental signaling rather than growth rate feedback

claim: Growing cells produce extra ribosomes in order to prepare for fluctuating conditions.
source: We suggest that growing cells produce extra ribosomes in order to prepare for fluctuating conditions.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the excess ribosome data

claim: If cells were to precisely tune their ribosomal content to express only the ribosomes needed for slow growing conditions, their level would limit the speed by which rapid growth could be resumed upon nutrients supply.
source: If cells were to precisely tune their ribosomal content to express only the ribosomes needed for the slow growing conditions, their level would limit the speed by which rapid growth could be resumed upon nutrients supply.
evidence: Logical inference about the consequences of not maintaining excess ribosomes

claim: The requirement to be prepared for fluctuating conditions affects the central cellular processes such as the coordination of ribosome production with growth rate.
source: Our study suggests that this requirement to be prepared for fluctuating conditions affects not only specific genes or pathways, but also the central cellular processes such as the coordination of ribosome production with growth rate.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the study's findings

claim: The proteome fraction coding for ribosomal proteins scales linearly with growth rate in budding yeast.
source: We find that also in budding yeast, the proteome fraction coding for ribosomal proteins scales linearly with the specific growth rate.
evidence: Supported by proteomic profiling data across multiple conditions

claim: The value of the slope is predicted by models of balanced growth to be precisely the time required for translation elongation of a full ribosome.
source: The value of this slope is predicted by models of balanced growth to be precisely the time required for translation elongation of a full ribosome.
evidence: Based on theoretical models of balanced growth

claim: Even rapidly growing cells still maintain ≈25% of their ribosomal proteins inactive.
source: Accordingly, even rapidly growing cells still maintain ≈25% of their ribosomal proteins inactive.
evidence: Calculated from proteomic and polysome profiling data

claim: The scaling curve observed, and in particular the fraction of residual, inactive ribosomes, is not an inherent unavoidable consequence of cell physiology or the mechanism of ribosome production, but is rather a consequence of signaling which sets the ratio of active vs. inactive ribosomes as a function of growth conditions.
source: These results imply that the scaling curve we observed, and in particular the fraction of residual, inactive ribosomes, is not an inherent unavoidable consequence of cell physiology or the mechanism of ribosome production, but is rather a consequence of signaling which sets the ratio of active vs. inactive ribosomes as a function of growth conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the alterability of the scaling relationship under different perturbations

claim: Monosomes consist of mRNA bound by a single ribosome and are thought to contain primarily inactive ribosomes.
source: In this method, the optical density of RNAs is quantified, with polysomes consisting of mRNA bound by multiple ribosomes. Most actively translating ribosomes are found in the polysomes while monosomes (mRNA with a single ribosome) are thought to contain primarily inactive ribosomes (Aspden et al., 2014; Castelli et al., 2011; Chassé et al., 2017; Kapp et al., 2004; Kelen et al., 2009; Liu and Qian, 2016; Warner et al., 1963).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations on polysome profiling interpretation

claim: The total length of rRNA in one ribosome is about 5500 bp.
source: The total length of rRNA in one ribosome is about 5500 bp while the average mRNA length is 1250 bp (Milo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milo et al., 2010

claim: The average mRNA length is 1250 bp.
source: The total length of rRNA in one ribosome is about 5500 bp while the average mRNA length is 1250 bp (Milo et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Milo et al., 2010

claim: The rRNA fraction of total RNA in monosomes is ~82%.
source: Accordingly, the rRNA fraction of total RNA in monosomes is ~82%, and in polysomes containing 5 ribosomes is ~96%.
evidence: Calculated from rRNA and mRNA lengths

claim: The rRNA fraction of total RNA in polysomes containing 5 ribosomes is ~96%.
source: Accordingly, the rRNA fraction of total RNA in monosomes is ~82%, and in polysomes containing 5 ribosomes is ~96%.
evidence: Calculated from rRNA and mRNA lengths

claim: All budding yeast strains in this study were based on BY4742 or Y8205 laboratory strains.
source: All budding yeast (S. cerevisiae) strains in this study were based on BY4742 (Brachmann et al., 1998) or Y8205 (Hin Yan Tong and Boone, 2005) laboratory strains.
evidence: Description of experimental strains used

claim: Mass-spectrometry analysis was employed to define the proteomic composition of S. cerevisiae cells growing in three conditions: standard media (SC), media low in nitrogen (Low N) and media low in phosphate (Low Pi).
source: We employed mass-spectrometry analysis to define the proteomic composition of S. cerevisiae cells growing in three conditions: standard media (SC), media low in nitrogen (Low N) and media low in phosphate (Low Pi).
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: The proteomic data was combined with published proteomic datasets of budding yeast growing on 12 different carbon sources.
source: This data was combined with published proteomic datasets of budding yeast growing on 12 different carbon sources (Paulo et al., 2015; 2016).
evidence: Description of data sources

claim: All profiles were calibrated with an external data reference defining absolute protein levels.
source: To avoid method-specific biases, all profiles were calibrated with an external data reference defining absolute protein levels (Wang et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of data normalization method
